scenes.title: Concept Explanation
scenes.speaker: AI Mentor
scenes.narration: Binary Search works by repeatedly halving a monotonically sorted search space. To do this correctly, we maintain three pointers: low, high, and mid. Every decision relies on comparing arr[mid] with your target.

scenes.title: Visual Animation: The Pointer Mechanics
scenes.speaker: AI Mentor
scenes.narration: Watch the pointers move in this live simulation. Our target is 23. Mid evaluates to 16. Since 16 is strictly less than 23, everything to the left of mid including mid itself is impossible. Low MUST advance to mid plus 1!

scenes.title: Your Specific Mistake Analyzed
scenes.speaker: AI Mentor
scenes.narration: In question FINAL-DSA-001, you chose an option that set low equals mid. Notice what happens when only two elements remain: low equals 0, high equals 1. Mid evaluates to 0. Setting low equals mid leaves low at 0 forever, triggering an infinite loop!

visualData.explanation: Search space never shrinks when mid rounds down to low.

scenes.title: The Correct Reasoning
scenes.speaker: AI Mentor
scenes.narration: Here is the mathematical truth: we already tested arr[mid] and proved it is NOT the target. Therefore, mid has zero chance of being the answer. We MUST discard mid completely by advancing low to mid plus 1!

scenes.title: Step-by-Step Code Walkthrough
scenes.speaker: AI Mentor
scenes.narration: Let's inspect the canonical while loop: while low is less than or equal to high. We calculate mid using low plus high minus low over 2, compare arr[mid] with target, and adjust low or high strictly past mid.

scenes.title: Common Traps & Edge Cases
scenes.speaker: AI Mentor
scenes.narration: Always remember two classic traps: First, never use (low + high) / 2 in 32-bit systems because it can overflow. Second, always use while (low <= high), not strictly less than, so single-element subranges get evaluated.

traps: Overflow trap: Always use low + (high - low) / 2
Boundary trap: Use low <= high so single elements are tested
Movement trap: Never write low = mid or high = mid

scenes.title: Quick Practice Check

scenes.narration: Quick question: If arr is [4, 7], target is 7, and mid is 0. Does low move to mid or mid plus 1? Mid plus 1! Low becomes 1, mid becomes 1, and target 7 is matched immediately!

scenes.title: Concept Synthesis
scenes.speaker: AI Mentor
scenes.narration: You now possess the exact mental model needed. Binary search guarantees O(log N) efficiency precisely because low and high shrink the candidate range without ever getting stuck.

scenes.narration: Look at the standard code on screen. In while low less than or equal to high: calculate mid, check if arr[mid] equals target, if smaller do low equals mid plus 1, else high equals mid minus 1. Simple, clean, and bug-free.

scenes.title: Common Traps & Edge Cases
scenes.speaker: AI Mentor (Indian English)
scenes.narration: Keep three important rules in mind: First, always use low plus high minus low by two to avoid integer overflow. Second, use low less than or equal to high so single elements are checked. And third, never write low equals mid.

traps: Overflow trap: Always use low + (high - low) / 2
Boundary trap: Use low <= high so single elements are tested
Movement trap: Never write low = mid or high = mid

scenes.title: Quick Practice Check on Screen
scenes.speaker: AI Mentor (Indian English)
scenes.narration: Now let us do a quick check on screen. If arr has elements 4 and 7, target is 7, and mid is 0. Where should low move? Select option B: low equals mid plus 1! Low moves to index 1, and target 7 is matched immediately!

scenes.title: Concept Synthesis: O(log N) Superpower
scenes.speaker: AI Mentor (Indian English)
scenes.narration: Because we divide the array in half every time, Binary Search has a time complexity of Big-O of log N. Even if you have 10 lakh elements — one million elements — it finds the answer in at most 20 comparisons! That is the power of logarithmic search.
